subtopic: MOTION TO AMEND STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this resolution is to set up a permanent committee on veterans affairs every year or every session when the other committees of the house are set up. To the man on the street this resolution may look rather complicated, but some of my lawyer friends have checked it and they tell me it is correct. I realize how lawyers can disagree on legal points, but I think this resolution is quite all right.
The Department of Veterans Affairs is one of the largest departments of the government,

Veterans Affairs
and it is only reasonable that it should have a committee associated with it. There are committees of the house which are not particularly important, but the veterans affairs committee would be important. Perhaps it might not be needed to sit every year, but it would always be there when needed. Veterans organizations and veterans generally would feel more secure if they knew they had the right to go to their member of parliament and have their case reviewed or dealt with by a committee of the house.
Some may say, what is wrong with things as they are? That may be all right for the present, but what of the future? In the short time I have been here we have had three ministers of veterans affairs. First there was the late Hon. Ian Mackenzie; then there was the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), followed by the present Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe). All those gentlemen were professional soldiers, and they knew the problems of the veterans from experience. But how long are we going to have men of this type holding the portfolio of veterans affairs minister? I personally hope it will be for a long time, but as the years go by the situation will change and most likely we will have a non-veteran minister or ministers.
A minister who has never seen active service can never be expected to understand the problems of the veteran the same as one who has had that experience. As time passes the administration can get farther away from the purposes of the acts which have been passed. After a number of years the people administering such legislation may forget the purposes and the reasons for the legislation and why it was passed. Our veterans, including those of world war I and world war II, constitute a significant proportion of the total Canadian population. Their problems are considerable and require constant attention. These problems could be dealt with much more effectively if the veterans had an opportunity to bring them before a standing committee through their members of parliament.
Furthermore, such a committee would facilitate the presentation of veterans problems by the Canadian Legion and other recognized veterans organizations in Canada. Often in the past there have been times when there has been no committee on veterans affairs, with the result that important problems affecting veterans and their families did not receive the proper airing to which they were entitled. The Department of Veterans Affairs acts in an administrative capacity in dealing with veterans problems. Competent as the department may be in this role, the fact is that our veterans require additional attention

which is beyond the scope of the administrators in the department.
Then there are the important matters of pensions and allowances which can be met only by appropriate changes in the veterans legislation. A standing committee could give frequent study to the Pension Act and the War Veterans Allowance Act as new developments arose to justify changes in the legislation. As it is now, the veterans affairs committee is set up only on the initiative of the government to deal with special matters. The members of parliament therefore are handicapped by not having up to date information pertaining to veterans and their problems. If a permanent committee was established and if it sat every parliamentary session, parliament would be in a much better position to determine when changes in veterans legislation were required.
I feel sure that a veterans affairs committee dealing with these matters from year to year would be able to see that the legislation passed for the benefit of the veterans was maintained and used for the benefit of the veterans. Only by having a permanent veterans affairs committee of the house which can keep the administration and the legislation close to the needs of the veteran are we going to get the kind of administration the veterans should have.
I move this resolution in the hope that the government will give it consideration in the near future. I could say a lot more about this resolution, but I know other hon. members will want to express their views on such an important matter as the setting up of a veterans affairs committee of the house. As the time allotted to this debate is limited I shall refrain from going into detail.
I hope the minister will be able to convince the government of the need of a standing committee on veterans affairs. I am trying to set a good example, and have made my remarks brief so the minister will have an opportunity in the short time during which this matter will be under discussion to get the views of hon. members, not only on the government side but on all sides of the house.

subtopic: MOTION TO AMEND STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak very briefly on this motion and to indicate the support of hon. members of this party. The resolution of the hon. member for Selkirk to set up a permanent committee on veterans affairs is not something new. While it may not have been the subject of discussion before on private members' day, it is a matter that has often been raised by individual members both in the house and on many occasions before the special committee on veterans affairs.

Each year members receive briefs from the large veterans organizations, and in addition they constantly receive communications from veterans organizations in their ridings. Many receive copies of resolutions passed by Legion branches in their ridings, all advocating that there should be a standing committee on veterans affairs.
It has been the custom for a number of years for the Canadian Legion to present a brief to the government each November, and each time a brief is presented it contains many important recommendations covering a very wide range of topics. They deal with important matters and issues affecting thousands of Canadian veterans both male and female, and their dependents. Therefore it would seem to me that no more suitable course could be followed than for the annual Legion brief to be referred to a standing committee on veterans affairs each year.
The brief submitted by the Legion last November, which no doubt has been read by many hon. members, covered a very wide range of topics. To itemize them briefly, it dealt with national defence, pensions, conditions not recorded on enlistment, revised rates for dependent parents, increase in pension to certain dependent parents, retroactive awards, debts due to the crown, supplementation to Canadian rates, war veterans allowance, veterans of world war I, widows of allied ex-servicemen, supplementation for orphans pensioned under the Canadian Pension Act, and the equity in a home, among other matters. In my opinion the Legion made very fair and reasonable recommendations with respect to these matters.
I am not suggesting that their brief will not receive every consideration from the minister and the officials of his department but, after all, there are in the house between 75 and 100 members who have seen service in different branches of our armed forces, and they are able to bring to such a committee a great amount of valuable experience. As far as I know I have never heard the present Minister of Veterans Affairs or any other minister of veterans affairs advance any reason or suggest any ground for objecting to a standing committee on veterans affairs. As we all know, at the present time there are quite a number of standing committees of the house, and if you review the records you will find that some of them have not had a single meeting in whole sessions.
As has been suggested by the hon. member for Selkirk, if we had such a committee its members could study the Legion briefs and bring to the attention of the committee the various matters involving veterans that come to their attention in their ridings. Today there are a large number of statutes
Veterans Affairs
having to do with the welfare of veterans and their dependents. This simply means that all the legislation affecting veterans should be constantly under review with the hope of improving it, amending the various acts so as to bring their benefits more in line with present day conditions and also removing from the present legislation anything that may work a hardship or injustice.
The Department of Veterans Affairs is a large spending department because of the substantial expenditure in pensions and war veterans allowances and, as was so well put forward by the previous speaker, it would appear most reasonable to me that there should be a standing committee for the department. I do not think the minister should take this suggestion as indicating in any way that there is anything wrong with the administration of the department. I think he should take the view that members of all parties in the house want to help the minister and provide the very best possible legislation for Canadian veterans.
Before this short debate is over I sincerely hope the minister will indicate that he will accept the resolution and is willing to recommend to the government the setting up of a standing committee on veterans affairs.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. G. J. Hahn (New Wesiminster):
subtopic: MOTION TO AMEND STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this group are very happy that the hon. member for Selkirk has seen fit to introduce this resolution at this time. I sincererly hope the minister, as suggested a moment ago by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, will be willing to accept the resolution in the spirit in which it is put forward, for I am quite sure from my past experience as a member of the special committee on veterans affairs that the resolution should be and probably will be supported by members on all sides of the house.
I hope to follow the example of the two hon. gentlemen who have preceded me so far as time is concerned, and I shall enunciate briefly some of the reasons why I feel it is desirable to set up such a committee. I consider that the Department of Veterans Affairs is just as important as any other department, and under these circumstances it would seem to me that we should have a standing committee in the same way that we have standing committees on miscellaneous private bills, marine and fisheries and other matters.
It is true that the special committee on veterans affairs is not set up each year, but it is also a fact that some of the standing committees do not sit during each session of parliament. There are frequent occasions when special cases arise which can be dealt with in the committee. Those who

Veterans Affairs
have been members of the special committee on veterans affairs will recognize that from time to time we do have cases involving special problems to bring to the attention of the minister and the representatives of his department. Actually such cases are dealt with best in a committee where we can speak directly to some of the members of his staff who are more familiar with these matters.
I was somewhat surprised, however, to hear the hon. gentleman who introduced this resolution suggest that one must be A veteran in order to understand veterans problems. I disagree with that suggestion. I will say this, however. It may be desirable to have members who are veterans on this committee that he suggests setting up. I trust I am not misinterpreting his suggestion, but I feel that if a standing committee is set up, certainly the best way to get some of the other members of this house who are not veterans to understand veterans problems is to have some of them on the committee. In that way they will get more familiar with the problems faced by veterans.
I am sure the house will agree with me when I say that those members of the special committees on veterans affairs who have not been veterans are certainly not those who held up legislation in so far as assistance to veterans is concerned. I believe this is also true of the members of this house. There are many non-veterans in the house, and they are certainly not opposed to veterans legislation merely because they are not veterans; nor are they opposed to it because they are not too familiar with the problems faced by veterans.
I also feel that the veterans as such must feel they are being placed in a secondary position by the members of this parliament who do not see fit to give them, with regard to a committee on veterans affairs, the same standing as, let us say, the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills, most of which are divorce bills. I do not think we should subject people who have served this country as well as have the veterans to being placed in the awkward position of having it suggested or even implied to them that they are not of as much importance as divorce cases, and that therefore we will not have a standing committee on veterans affairs for them. The same thing applies to the standing committee on marine and fisheries. I realize that these committees are necessary, but I definitely would agree with the hon. member who introduced this resolution that it is most essential and desirable that we should have a standing committee on veterans affairs. We in this group will support his resolution.

subtopic: MOTION TO AMEND STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the minister speaks I want to submit a few ideas that might possibly alter what he is going to say. However, I want to make it clear at the outset that I am giving my complete moral support to the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Selkirk. After thinking the matter over carefully, and having myself been privileged to serve on two of the veterans committees in the present parliament, while I realize a good many of the arguments there are on the other side, especially the argument that there are too many committees already and that at certain times of the year we all have more committees than we can attend, nevertheless it seems to me that on balance the advantage is definitely on the side of having a permanent standing committee of this house on veterans affairs, if for no other reason than that it would tend to remove any suggestion of discrimination there might be in the minds of some of the veterans of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I want to make it clear that in my opinion Canada has now and has had for a good many years the best all-round veterans legislation of any country which I have been privileged to study. I think our veterans legislation is better than that of any other country I know of. I think it is better than even that of our great, good and rich neighbour to the south, namely the republic of the United States of America. One reason it is good, I believe, is that we have always had in this house a large number of people who were intimately acquainted with veterans problems and who kept in touch with them. We have had a sensitive public opinion throughout the whole of Canada. We have had an alert press; and of course we have had vigilant veterans organizations who themselves are on the job. The whole thing has combined, I think, to give this country the best veterans legislation of any country in the western world.
I can remember what was said in one of the very few but very fine speeches made by the late hon. member for Halton, the late Miss Sybil Bennett. In a brief speech one day-one of her rare speeches in the house- I can remember she said what a thrill it had given her to see how all the parties in this house treated veterans legislation on a completely impartial basis.
I am not going to say that my own experience in veterans affairs committees has been quite that fortunate. I say that in the veterans committee there have been times when some people played politics; and for all I know, if we had this veterans committee as a standing committee, if it sat in election years perhaps people would have more of the same

tendency to play politics that they had at other times. But on balance I do not believe that is a valid objection. I have watched them in action and noted members like the hen. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), whom I have always seen in the veterans committee being absolutely fair and impartial, not grinding any political axe, even when he has to be fair to the government.
I believe those precedents would be carried out if we had the veterans committee set up as a permanent institution to sit if necessary from year to year. I am not convinced that even if we had a veterans committee set up as a permanent institution, it would necessarily have to sit every single year. But even if it had to sit to deal with only a few minor matters, I believe it would be useful as a discussion agency in order to bring out the points that need bringing out.
I would not want anyone to run away with the idea that because I am in favour of this resolution suggested by the hon. member for Selkirk, I am even implying that there is any lethargy or indifference on the part of the government, and certainly not on the part of the Minister of Veterans Affairs. To the best of my memory I do not recall within the last 25 or 30 years our having a bad or indifferent minister of veterans affairs, but in all honesty I believe we have never had a better Minister of Veterans Affairs than we have right at this moment.

I agree with him that our veterans legislation will compare favourably with any other veterans legislation in the world. There is a reason for that, and I will go into it more fully later.
I am sure the minister welcomes this resolution. Reading the press recently one finds that the main slogan of the government at the present time, and for certain reasons, is national unity. I am sure, following that idea through, the minister would be glad to unite the members of this house on a nonpartisan basis into a committee to assist him and his department in the handling of the difficulties that face his department and the veterans organizations in the future. I am sure the minister will welcome this committee, because it affords an opportunity to share responsibilities in a matter that is beyond the realm of politics. I believe most of the veterans in Canada, and most of the members of this house who are veterans, do all they can to keep veterans problems outside the realm of politics.
Perhaps the reason our legislation can compare favourably with that of any other country in the world is that very early in the last war the government set up a veterans affairs committee for the purpose of opening up the old acts as they applied to veterans of the first war, and relating them to the new forces. This was a committee to develop a program of pension adjustments, veterans allowances and so on, with respect to the new forces. The committee could initiate ideas and recommend a rehabilitation program. The committee sat continuously and was not, as it has been in the last several years, merely a committee to examine legislation.
During the past several years the committee that has been set up has been limited to the examination of certain legislation the government was introducing. The committee was powerless to make amendments, but could make recommendations that were tabled

Veterans Affairs
in the house. The committee which related the old acts to the new forces and expanded them had a rather free hand. I know, because I sat on that committee all during the war. It was a process of continual study, amendment or expansion of the acts and the development of a whole rehabilitation program that had to do with demobilization, education, the Veterans' Land Act and all the rest of them. It is for that reason our legislation was hammered into the shape it was when the war finally finished.
I believe if I were the minister of veterans affairs I would be quite pleased to get a committee of that kind to share responsibility with me. The pension commission and others who administer different acts under the minister's department should welcome this committee. They have many administrative difficulties that are not understood either by members of the house or the public. If we had a continuing committee people would be able to come to us and point out their difficulties. Most of the members of this house have opinions which would be of great benefit in considering legislation that is being demanded. So far as I am concerned I have always taken the position this is a nonpartisan problem, and if there are demands made which I think are unrealistic or cannot be supported by the facts-and I think this applies to most members of the committee-I have had no hesitation in saying so. I am sure that with all the books the minister has in front of him he has come prepared to give us the legal arguments and the reasons why this committee should be welcomed with open arms. I am quite sure he is going to do that.
If one takes a look at the brief that was presented to the cabinet in December, 1956, by the Legion, one finds it indicates the need for a continuing study of veterans problems. There is no doubt that the Legion officials did a lot of research in the preparation of that brief, but at the present time most of the members of this house are not in a position to say whether or not those demands are reasonable or economic. There are many demands for changes in the Pension Act, such as the dependents' pensions. Apparently someone did some work on the percentage difference between wages that were paid at the time these acts were set up and the increases that have taken place in wages since, to indicate that the rates paid today, based on the formula that was adopted at the time the acts were set up, are completely out of line. The War Veterans Allowance Act, the matter of permissible earnings

those things have all been gone into again, and there are many demands in the brief.
I believe there are two departments of government that absolutely need a continuing

committee, one of which is veterans affairs. Veterans affairs is going to be a continuing problem as long as anyone in this house lives. There is no finality to it. If the country is going to prosper and we are going to have twice as much money to spend in 1980 as we have today, as the Gordon commission suggests, then veterans legislation has to keep pace with that. It is not going to remain static.
As I say, there is no finality to this problem. There should be a continuous study made by members of this house, in co-operation with the members of the commission, if the members of the house are going to be informed sufficiently to vote according to the social and economic values of the problems facing them.
Unless we have the opportunity of studying the matter there is not much chance of a person in this house passing an intelligent vote on the problem.
About the only way that I see it can be done is through a veterans affairs committee. In that committee there would be available to the members experts from all branches of the department. The department is in housing today, and in land settlement. It is handling great social and economic problems. A terrific job is being done by the Department of Veterans Affairs. I think the minister needs help. I believe the people in all branches of the commission who have the responsibility of making decisions on veterans affairs have a right to inform members of this house as to the difficulties of administration, and to get the understanding co-operation at least of the members of the house.
An odd time in that committee you will find a member or two who wants to make capital out of its deliberations. That is a very small percentage of the committee. Many subjects are discussed, and no matter what kind of group you get together you find one or two who just do not play the game according to the rules, but it is a very small percentage. My experience on the committee has shown me that it is as non-partisan as a committee of this house could possibly be. So far as I am concerned it has always been the desire of the committee to help the veterans, but to be reasonable and understanding with respect to demands made on the public treasury.
I believe the permissive earnings and the war veterans allowances are burning questions. These questions need a lot of study. I believe the government has been unrealistic so far as that particular legislation is concerned. Then there is the matter of expanding the War Veterans Allowance

Act to include England as a theatre of war for world war I veterans. They are running out. There is still a large number who should be receiving the war veterans allowance. There is discrimination as between the younger and the older veterans. These are matters that should be, and I believe could be, ironed out by a committee.
As I said a moment ago, and I want to reiterate it, with the development of this country forecast for the future, with the advance in income and the increase in the standard of living, if the veterans-and there is a large number of them today-are to go forward and enjoy a share of that prosperity there has to be a continued study and revision of the acts having to do with veterans, in order to keep the veteran in the same relative position as he is today with respect to incomes and standards. The only way to do that is by constant study and revision and the application of increased rates to acts that have to do with the welfare and the future of veterans.
I have been deliberately brief in my remarks, because I want to give the minister a chance to advance to his own colleagues all the arguments he has at his disposal as to why the government should give him some assistance by passing some of the responsibilities of his department on to the members of the house. In that way we may lighten his burden a little. It would enable the staffs who administer the different acts to get the opinions of members and others about their difficulties, so we may have some understanding of what they are up against.

subtopic: MOTION TO AMEND STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you know suggestions have been made in this house for several years and by members on all sides that a standing committee on veterans affairs should be set up. That request has been made not only in the house, it has also been made by the different veterans organizations across Canada. For example, at the dominion convention of the Canadian Legion, which was held in Vancouver last June, this resolution was adopted:
Whereas the government has not seen fit to appoint a committee on veterans affairs during the present session of parliament;
Whereas problems are continually arising concerning the Pension Act, War Veterans Allowance Act, et cetera;
Be it resolved that this convention make representations for the appointment of a permanent standing committee on veterans affairs to which all such problems would be referred.
I believe the time has now come when this action could be taken, and I hope the Minister of Veterans Affairs will be in a position this evening to announce that the
Veterans Affairs
government has changed its stand on this particular question, and that from now on we can have such a committee. You see, Mr. Speaker, the request is not made in a frivolous way; it is made because the only way the veterans problems can be dealt with fully and adequately is by having a committee of this house which meets every year.
The practice in the past has been to set up a special committee only when there was significant veterans legislation coming before the house. For example, last session there was no such committee, although there were two or three minor bills having to do with veterans affairs. This year there is no hint that there will be any legislation having to do with veterans at all and, of course, there is no hint of a committee. But whether or not there is legislation-and I regret very much if there is to be none at this present session-such a committee could do valuable work.
I do not intend to go over the arguments which have been put forward already this evening in a very capable way by different hon. members, but there are these facts to remember. The veterans are affected by a variety of statutes of this parliament. For example, there are the Pension Act, the War Veterans Allowance Act and the Veterans' Land Act. In addition to these and other statutes there are regulations passed under the act setting up the department, which are of great importance. For example, there are the treatment regulations under which all the veteran's who go into hospital have to come in order to get their hospitalization.
Then there are a tremendous number of Canadians involved. I suppose the veterans of the two world wars and their dependents would number well over a million. The number may be much larger than that. These veterans and their dependents are affected in a very personal way. It is not as though there was something more or less indirect in it. Their whole lives are affected directly by this legislation and by these regulations.
The veterans of Canada have been very fortunate to be represented for many years by organizations which are thoroughly responsible and statesmanlike. Take for example the Canadian Legion and the National Council of Veterans Associations in Canada, which is composed of the Army, Navy and Air Force Veterans in Canada, the Canadian Corps Association, the Canadian Paraplegic Association, the Sir Arthur Pearson Association of War Blinded, War Amputations of Canada and the War Pensioners of Canada. All these organizations, as everyone in this house will admit, have dealt with the problems facing the veteran down through the

Veterans Affairs
years in a statesmanlike way, and they are doing so today. They feel, however, just as hon. members of the house feel who are asking for this committee, that the problems are changing continuously. There is always a need to meet some new situation which is arising. It is mainly for that reason we urge tonight that there should be set up now a standing committee on veterans affairs.
We have the example, Mr. Speaker, of the standing committee on external affairs. It took some years to get agreement for the setting up of that committee, but it has functioned in a successful way from the start. The estimates of the Department of External Affairs are referred to that committee every year. The minister appears and gives evidence, as does the deputy minister and various other officials of the department; in fact I think any official of whom the committee members request an appearance. Furthermore, legislation is referred to that committee. Your Honour will remember that two years ago the international river improvements bill was referred to the external affairs committee and dealt with there in a very efficient manner.
I see no reason why the same thing could not be done in establishing a standing committee on veterans affairs. Each year the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs could be referred to that committee, and legislation could also be referred. Not only could officials be heard, but we could also have representatives from these veterans organizations who have always been invited to appear before the special committees. There is no reason why they could not appear just as well before a standing committee each year. If this course were followed the result would be to keep the veterans legislation up to date and, as some hon. members have mentioned, it would assist in rectifying any mistakes.
Further, I think it would help to keep the administration of these acts human. I am not contending tonight that the officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs are not human in their dealings with the veterans, but it would help to keep that spirit prevailing throughout the whole department in the branches from coast to coast if we had a committee meeting every year dealing with the different problems.
Finally, I suggest that by setting up a committee we would give parliament its proper place in connection with veterans affairs. Parliament has not been drawn into the picture as fully as it should have been, because there has only been a committee established infrequently. If there is to be no legislation concerning veterans this year it will mean there can be no improvement in the benefits
TMr. Green.]
for the veterans of Canada and their dependents until 1958. If unfortunately that is to be the case, then I hope this parliament in its dying days can at least make sure that from now on there will be a standing committee on veterans affairs.

subtopic: MOTION TO AMEND STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to give my wholehearted support to the resolution moved by the hon. member for Selkirk, which in effect asks for the establishment of a standing committee of this house on veterans affairs. I am always interested when I follow the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra in these debates, because he and I got cold feet together in the same trenches about 41 years ago. Little idea had we at that time that we would be pleading in this house in support of a resolution of this nature.
I support this resolution for three reasons in particular. The first is that as a result of my 12 years' experience in this house and my experience over that period in the special committee on veterans affairs when it was sitting, I am convinced of the need for this standing committee to which the recurring problems of veterans and their dependents can be referred. Anyone who served on that committee throughout that period realizes that' the amendments made to legislation since 1945 resulted largely from the representations made by the Canadian Legion and other veterans organizations, and the consideration given to those representations by that committee.
My second reason for supporting this resolution is that the Canadian Legion, the National Council of Veterans Associations and the organizations of which it is composed have a very close knowledge of the needs of veterans and their dependent's in this country. At repeated national, provincial and local conventions of these organizations resolutions have been passed urging the establishment of a standing committee on veterans affairs. That opinion was expressed again at the last national convention of the Canadian Legion, when a resolution was adopted in almost similar terms to those adopted in previous years, asking the government to establish a standing committee on veterans affairs.
My third reason for supporting the resolution is one advanced by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. That is because the veterans and their dependents represent a very large segment of the Canadian population. I would say, as the hon. member did, that well over one million people are involved in this question, and we have a particular responsibility to those people. Veterans and their dependents in Canada are

entitled to particular consideration by hon. members of this house and the government.
The present veterans legislation is excellent, I know. As I have said before, our legislation in Canada is possibly the best total veterans legislation in the western democratic world. I realized that very much when I was in Great Britain last summer and had the opportunity to discuss this matter with some of the former high command of the British army, who were very complimentary about our legislation in Canada and critical of the legislation in existence in Great Britain. Certainly we should do this. We are in a land rich in natural resources and with a relatively small population. To do what we have done for veterans and their dependents throughout the years has been much easier for us in Canada than it would be for a country like Great Britain during that time.
We have no criticism of the officials of the department. I have had a great deal of experience with the officials of the various branches of the Department of Veterans Affairs. I have always found them courteous and willing to do all they could for the veterans within the terms of the law and the regulations. We do believe, however, that because veterans problems are naturally in a fluid state due to changing conditions and circumstances, there should be an opportunity to review these questions before a standing committee of this house at least yearly.
To prove that contention I will indicate the number of resolutions that were passed on various aspects of veterans legislation at the last' dominion convention of the Canadian Legion.
Mind you, these resolutions come from the branches of the Canadian Legion, from the branches of the national council of veterans across Canada. They flow from the local branches to the provincial commands to the national conventions, and they are the result of people in the various communities, other veterans, appreciating the difficulties of the veterans and their dependents and the deficiencies in the present legislation, and the need for amendments to correct the situation.
What do we find? At the last dominion convention of the Canadian Legion there were 22 resolutions submitted seeking amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act, some of somewhat major importance and some of somewhat minor importance. They were submitted because of the belief that the legislation required amending in order to adequately serve veterans and their dependents.
Veterans Affairs
There were 20 resolutions submitted with respect to amendments to the Canadian Pension Act and dealing with various aspects of that important piece of legislation, which is indeed an excellent act. Those were sought because of changing conditions and circumstances, and the fact that from year to year it is found that certain aspects of the legislation do not work correctly and do not give the veterans the justice they deserve. Consequently, at the last dominion convention of the Canadian Legion there were 20 resolutions submitted calling for amendments to the Canadian Pension Act.
Then there were 21 resolutions dealing with the treatment of veterans and the treatment regulations, a most important aspect of veterans affairs legislation. The conditions, circumstances and problems in connection with treatment are constantly changing, and because of that we had these 21 resolutions presented to the convention.
Then we had five resolutions dealing with problems of the imperial veterans, something which needs serious consideration. Hon. members of this house representing all parties have advanced pleas on behalf of certain imperial veterans, and because of that we had a recent amendment to the War Veterans Allowance Act which brought under the legislation those imperial veterans who had resided in Canada for 20 years.
There were five resolutions presented at the convention dealing with rehabilitation problems. As the date of the second world war recedes the number of resolutions of this character are lessening, but regardless of that fact there were five resolutions dealing with rehabilitation problems affecting the veteran.
Then there were two resolutions dealing with amendments to the Veterans' Land Act. Why? While this legislation is effective and is serving a great purpose, experience and changing circumstances prove the need for some amendments.
Then there were five resolutions adopted with respect to the armed forces and civil defence. Those resolutions were put forward by local branches because the members understood the problems of men presently in the armed forces. There were eight resolutions dealing with the Canadian civil service, seeking to correct certain things which need correcting. There were over 30 resolutions dealing with miscellaneous problems which were of particular interest to veterans and their dependents, such as the Last Post fund, headstones for veterans, Remembrance day and so on.

Veterans Affairs
When such a large number of resolutions were presented to the last dominion convention of the Canadian Legion recommending amendments to veterans legislation, it would surely indicate the necessity for a standing committee of this house to review the legislation, to hear representations by veterans organizations, and to make recommendations to this house. If we can have a standing committee of this house to deal exclusively with the problem of providing ourselves with provender in the restaurant, which I think is a somewhat minor matter compared with the problems of veterans and their dependents, surely we are justified in asking for a standing committee on veterans affairs at this time.
We have a number of standing committees which meet only rarely. I have been a member of the standing committee on mines, forests and waters since 1945, and it has never met during that whole period. That committee is supposed to deal with important problems, and I have suggested repeatedly that it should meet. The committee on mines, forests and waters deals with natural resources, in which I am very interested; but here we have human problems affecting large numbers of Canadians and which occur from day to day, from week to week, from month to month and from year to year.
We on this side of the house, and on the other side as well, who are urging the establishment of this standing committee on veterans affairs do so because we believe the problems of the veterans and their dependents deserve the consideration of this house through the establishment of a standing committee on veterans affairs. As one or two speakers have mentioned previously, the Department of Veterans Affairs is a very important department. Its estimates this year are somewhat over $250 million, which indicates the importance of the problems that exist across this country.
In conclusion I urge the minister to give consideration to supporting this resolution, the purpose of which is to try to get this government to accept its full responsibility by the establishment of this committee to meet the problems of veterans and their dependents which arise from year to year.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 want to speak only briefly on this matter. My first words shall be of congratulation to the hon. member for Selkirk upon introducing this resolution. I have not had the advantage, as have many of the previous speakers, of having sat on the special committee on veterans affairs, but over the years I have been closely connected with
[Mr. Herridge.l
the educational features of some of the programs initiated by the Department of Veterans Affairs and I think I know something of the problems that exist.
I do not intend to repeat the eulogies that have been fairly general about the administration of the department and the excellence of the legislation. As I listened to the arguments advanced by my colleagues I tried to discover what particular difference there was between a standing committee and a special committee on veterans affairs, which latter committee is called from time to time as its services are required. On the whole I think a case has been made for a standing committee. The concluding sentence or two of the previous speaker indicated that there are a great many veterans and dependents who are affected by the regulations of the Department of Veterans Affairs, and because there are so many of them and because their problems are so numerous a standing committee of this house was required.
Frequently we as members receive various resolutions from the branches of the Legion.
Not so long ago when I made a speech in the house in favour of increases in disability pensions as against increases in war veterans allowances I recall that, to use a slang expression, I got my tail in the gate, because I suggested at that time that if so many of the recipients of war veterans allowance were in fact affected by war service they should be getting disability pensions, and I still think that is correct. It is because there are problems of that kind which could be discussed more fully and adequately in a standing committee that I support the motion advanced tonight.
It has been stated that it would be an education for non-veterans to be on such a committee. I quite agree; but I suggest that in all fairness veterans are perhaps more competent persons to be selected for that committee. I said I was going to speak briefly, and I believe I have done so. I simply say that on balance I think a standing committee is what we should have. I point out to hon. members that it is not certain that a standing committee would necessarily be called to meet at every session of parliament, but it would give an opportunity to the minister when legislation is introduced to refer such legislation to a committee already in existence; therefore I support the resolution.

subtopic: MOTION TO AMEND STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as time is somewhat limited I am going to be very brief in my remarks. I support fully the setting up of a standing committee on veterans affairs. I believe if such a committee were allowed to investigate any

branch of the Department of Veterans Affairs year by year, and to hear briefs from veterans organizations, the committee could and probably would remain a truly non-partisan committee. I have been a member of veterans affairs committees for the past 20 years, and in my opinion the veterans affairs committees of recent years have not been nearly as non-partisan as they used to be.
During the war, as the hon. member for Cape Breton South stated, we had a committee that sat year by year, and it was given the responsibility of formulating a veterans charter around a number of draft bills. That committee was truly a non-partisan committee. Our one objective was to get the best charter we could for the veterans. I do not remember at any time any one party trying in any way to seek political advantage over another. But, unfortunately, after the war the government's policy with regard to a veterans affairs committee changed. No longer were we given a veterans affairs committee with wide open terms of reference. We were limited to very narrow terms of reference. Consequently, as soon as the committee met its members started to fight and wrangle in order to try to get the terms of reference extended, and so before the committee had sat for more than a few days it had become extremely partisan.
In my opinion the best way to prevent that happening would be to set up a standing committee on veterans affairs with wide open terms of reference, so it could deal with any branch of the Department of Veterans Affairs. Then once again I think we would have a truly non-partisan veterans affairs committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hour is getting late, but even at the risk of repeating statements already made I think it is desirable that, within the time limit, as many members as possible express their views on this most important resolution and let the minister know that on both sides of the house there are members with experience on the special committees of the past who believe that now is the time that a standing committee on veterans affairs should be established. It is for that reason, to add my voice to the arguments already put forward, that I rise to announce that I support the resolution.
I have only one possibly new point to submit. I believe, now that all our veterans are getting older and are finding conditions more difficult, that the setting up of a standing committee would raise the morale of many of these older veterans, because they would
Veterans Affairs
feel that they had a group of members of parliament who were making a special study of their problems and would be available so that they could present their particular points of view to the committee. I am not suggesting that every individual veteran with a problem would appear before the committee, but the veterans have their organizations, and through the representatives of those organizations they would be able to appear before the committee.
I am not going to take any more time, because I hope other members will speak. I hope the minister will explain his position, and that his reaction will be favourable.

Having listened carefully to the arguments that have been presented, I must say that frankly I cannot agree that any proof has been presented that a standing committee on veterans affairs would make any substantial or constructive contribution to the handling of veterans problems by parliament.
The hon. member for Kootenay West mentioned a number of reasons why he thought a standing committee would be a good idea. I tried to follow his reasoning, and a good example of it was that if parliament had a standing committee to operate the restaurant m order to provide, as he stated, comestibles for ourselves, we should have a standing committee on veterans affairs because it was a very much more important matter. I think that is a good example of the kind of argumentation that has been put forward in support of the resolution.
Of course the facts are that the reason for having a committee on the restaurant has nothing to do with its relative importance to any other problem in the country, whether local or national. As all hon. members know, the reason we have a committee on the restaurant is that there is nobody else to run the restaurant of parliament but parliament itself.
I think it is stretching logic and credulity to a great extent to make the kind of argument the hon. member made, namely that

Veterans Affairs
the fact that we had a committee on the restaurant in some way or other indicated that we felt that the provision of food for ourselves was more important than the matter of veterans affairs. The importance of veterans affairs has been recognized by all members of this parliament and by all parties in this house. I think service on the special committees on veterans affairs has been one of the real privileges enjoyed by a number of the members of this house. I know their privilege of serving on those special committees has been jealously guarded by the members concerned, and that many other members in this house would have felt it an equal privilege and would have wished the opportunity of giving similar service.
The membership of these committees has always been made up of members who are in fact veterans with military service either in world war I or world war II. In this debate it has been suggested that this exclusive membership is perhaps not necessary. I think the fact that the special committee has been made up wholly of veterans has been of advantage to the veterans in this country, because the members of that committee, themselves being veterans, have brought to their work in the committee specialized knowledge of the nature and real extent of the individual problems of veterans which we can hope to solve by providing the appropriate kind of legislation to deal with those problems.

speechtext:
My experience with the membership of these committees is that all the members have been veterans. I think that is proper and justifiable in the case of special committees. As all hon. members know, the membership of special committees is a matter which is given particular attention by the whips, and great care is taken to see that the membership of special committees is the best that can be secured.
I do not think it would be justifiable to apply a similar principle to any standing committee of this house. I think the membership of standing committees should be open to any member who wishes to serve on them and whose membership on such committees is convenient to the particular group in the house to which he belongs. I think in all probability a standing committee would lose much of the quality that the special committees have enjoyed.
All members with great unanimity and, I think, with equal justice have spoken of the veterans charter which was to a large extent the result of the work of the special veterans committee, the excellence of the veterans legislation we enjoy in this country, and the program we have for veterans welfare. To hon. members who have been supporting the idea of a special committee I should simply like to point out that this excellent position, this situation which they have all cited with some satisfaction and pride, has been achieved without the necessity of a standing committee which they now appear to try to suggest is essential for a continuation of this program. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the very proposal they have put forward and some of the grounds on which they try to justify it disprove their argument rather than establish it.
What would be the utility of a standing committee in this parliament? It has been suggested that it would give an opportunity for representatives of the Canadian Legion and other veterans groups to make representations and submissions. May I point out that these groups have for many years been making annual submissions and representations to the cabinet. All members of this house receive copies of these representations. There is certainly no validity in the suggestion that the contents of these submissions would be any more readily accessible to members by reason of a standing committee, rather than their getting copies of these submissions which are annually made to the cabinet and the excellent information that the Legion and

other veterans organizations make available to every member of this house.
Several hon. members have spoken of the excellent administration of the department and the manner in which veterans problems have been dealt with by the various branches of the department and the Canadian pension commission. Certainly it has been my experience, Mr. Speaker, that any information I or any other member of the house desires is readily available by asking the necessary question in the house or by correspondence with the department. No additional information would be available to any hon. member through the sittings of the standing committee. I have also found that when members proffer advice to the department, that advice is carefully taken into consideration and, if found appropriate, is acted upon.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra suggested that a standing committee was the proper place for matters of veterans affairs to be discussed. I do not doubt that, if there were a standing committee, it would be an excellent place for the discussion of matters relating to veterans. But, Mr. Speaker, it is my view that the best place and the proper place for members to express their views in connection with veterans affairs is in this house, and not simply in a committee of this house.
Parliament itself provides all the opportunities that any hon. member opposite could reasonably ask for expressing his views. The hon. member also said that he thought a standing committee would ensure the continuity of the humanitarian approach by officials of the department. I, for one, see no sign of any tendency for that humanitarian approach, to which he paid tribute, to weaken in any respect.
I do not know whether my experience as a member of this house has been much different from that of any other member, but as I listened to hon. members opposite I was thinking that it seemed to me what they really had in mind was a standing committee to provide a forum where individual problems with respect to the administration of veterans legislation would be dealt with. I submit, Mr. Speaker, if that is what they have in mind, that is not the proper function of either a standing committee or a special committee of this house.

I am sorry to say this has not always been the case in this house. I am not a veteran, so I would not expect to be a member of that committee. However, I have had a lot of work to do for the veterans. When I came here in 1940, about 75 per cent of the work we had to do in this house was for returned men, because they were coming back from the war and had to be rehabilitated. It was for that reason that I had a lot of work to do for the veterans.
I cannot understand why the Minister of Veterans Affairs objects to this standing committee. It would help him and it would help the house arrive at correct solutions for many of these problems. I do not wish to take up too much of the time of the house, because I should like to see a vote on the resolution. subtopic: MOTION TO AMEND STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
First of all I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Selkirk, who sponsored this resolution. I think the debate in the house tonight has been very constructive, but I am only going to take a few minutes because I know there are other members who want to speak. I should like to compliment most sincerely the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I think this minister, who goes about his work unobtrusively, is nevertheless one of the most effective ministers we have in the cabinet. I think this whole house should applaud the minister for the excellent work he has done.
The point I should like to raise is that the establishment of a standing committee does not necessarily mean it will be sitting at every session. For example, I believe the hon. member for Kootenay West pointed out that the committee on mines, forests and waters has not met in 17 years. I, Mr. Speaker, am a member of the radio and television committee, and certainly I think all hon. members will admit that committee has been very active. Yet it is a special

committee which is set up during a legislative period, and is not a standing committee. A special committee can always be convened and legislation can always be referred to it, or it can hear anything that comes up pertaining to a special subject. I believe that has been overlooked by some of the hon. members opposite.
I am happy to see that all members of the house have paid tribute to the magnificent program for veterans which we have in this country. I think the hon. member for Kootenay West referred to it as excellent and possibly the best total legislation for veterans in the western world. I am fully in agreement-and this is a non-partisan point- and I think everybody in this house is proud of what this government and this house have done for veterans in this country.
Certainly it would seem that, particularly in the matter of education, the veterans have been treated extremely well. Last year I referred to the fact that between 1942 and 1955 some $220 million was expended to assist veterans, which amounts to an average of about $16,900,000 every year over that period. This is only one particular facet of assistance to veterans. One needs only to mention the war gratuities and, of course, the last thing this parliament dealt with was the war veterans allowances.
I think my job as a member of this house, Mr. Speaker, is to do everything I possibly can for veterans and for the veterans in my riding; because certainly, as the hon. member who just took his seat said, the veterans deserve absolutely the best. They offered their lives to preserve our way of life. If I thought this resolution introduced by the hon. member would add to that I would think it could be supported. But, Mr. Speaker, as I say, certainly a special committee can be convened at any time. I think all members will agree that the veterans legislation of Canada is the best in the world. As I say, it is non-partisan. We all know that; we all agree. I would think the minister and the department are to be complimented most highly, in that the procedure we have now is the best possible way of handling the affairs of veterans.

subtopic: MOTION TO AMEND STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to be very brief. I did not want to speak on this because the previous speakers for my party have given their views very well on behalf of the veterans, and have said that their problems should be attended to without any delay.
The last speaker spoke as if nothing could be improved. The veteran finds himself in the position that prices are rising and he is not thought of at all. All we want today is

to have a committee to which we can appeal at all times on behalf of the veterans of this country. We do not want a special committee; we want a permanent committee that will be there all the time. We must realize that the cost of living is rising for the veteran. Those who are on pension are not receiving adequate pensions, and we should have a committee to deal with it immediately. A permanent committee should be set up to deal with the problems of every pensionable person in Canada, the aged, the crippled and the blind. They are waiting for election day. The government in power may do something two days before the election, but in the meantime the veterans can starve to death. That is their attitude. We want a permanent committee for those who cannot defend themselves.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to be very brief. I know the minister needs only five minutes to rise in his place and say that he and the government intend to endorse this resolution. Therefore I do riot think he needs every minute. However, I hope the sample of whitewash and red herring that came out of Halifax does not represent the attitude of the government toward this resolution, because if it does I am sure it will be most bitterly resented by the veterans of Canada.
When the senior hon. member for Halifax states that parliament presents any reasonable opportunity for discussion I believe I can readily deny that. This session of parliament is not meant to provide the veterans of Canada, or their spokesmen in this house, with such a reasonable opportunity. With all the problems of Canada the veterans and other problems which are urgent and pressing are relegated to the background, and we shall not be able to discuss them before the plug is pulled and we shall be asked to face an election. A standing committee of this house, as is proposed by this resolution, would be able to deal with all the usually reasonable representations of the Canadian Legion. They would not have to deal only with the proposals of the government in regard to veterans problems.
I think while the committees in the past have done excellent work they have always been handicapped in that it was the government that decided what field they might take into consideration. The over-all attitude of the people of the country and of hon. members to the very reasonable demands the Canadian Legion has made for many years now is one of sincere sympathy, and I feel that a standing committee could render great
Veterans Affairs
service and more closely examine the many complex problems the veterans face.

I am attempting to continue my remarks. I know my hon. friend who interrupts keeps the house long enough when he rises to his feet, and I wish he would allow me to complete my comments.
What is the procedure of the house under the standing orders as we have them? Standing order 65 is the one that deals with standing parliamentary committees. It sets out that at the commencement of every session the house shall form what we call a striking committee to determine the membership of the various standing committees. Then it proceeds to enumerate what are those standing committees, of which there are 12 in this house, the balance being joint committees with the other place. That is all, Mr. Speaker, that exists under this standing order.
I certainly wish to be corrected if my interpretation of the parliamentary procedure is wrong but these committees are nothing more than agencies of this house. They have no authority to do anything whatsoever, to initiate any legislation or to pass on anything, unless it has been referred by this house; and the authority they possess is given by this house. It was given this year on January 24. This is the practice which has always been followed in this house and is part of our established practice.
After the report of the striking committee enumerating the membership of the standing committees is brought forward-it is usually th^ practice to have the government whip do this-the leader of the government, the Prime Minister, moves:
That the standing committees of this house shall severally be empowered to examine and inquire into all such matters and things as may be referred to them by the house; and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon, with power to send for persons, papers and records.
These are the words which give authority to parliamentary committees, and a motion in this language can be found at page 589 of Hansard for January 24, 1957.
